title: The Basic Differential Pair
intro: Two matched transistors sharing a tail current source amplify the difference between two inputs and reject what they have in common.

blocks.text: A differential circuit processes the difference Vin1 - Vin2 and ignores a signal common to both inputs. That rejects supply noise, substrate coupling and common-mode interference, doubles the usable swing, gives better linearity (even-order distortion cancels) and biases more simply. For these reasons most modern analog circuits are differential.

Let the two gates be Vin1 and Vin2, the sources join at a node driven by a tail current ISS. If Vin1 is much greater than Vin2 the first transistor carries all of ISS. At equal inputs each carries ISS/2. In between the current steers smoothly from one side to the other.

blocks.alt: Schematic of a differential pair. Two NMOS transistors M1 and M2 have their sources joined and connected to a tail current source ISS to ground. Each drain connects to the supply VDD through its own resistor RD. The two gates are the differential inputs and the two drains are the differential outputs.
blocks.caption: The basic differential pair. The tail current ISS is steered between the two branches in proportion to the input difference.

blocks.source:
ID1 - ID2 = (1/2)*mu_n*Cox*(W/L) * Vid * sqrt( 4*ISS/(mu_n*Cox*(W/L)) - Vid^2 )     for |Vid| <= sqrt(2*ISS/(mu_n*Cox*W/L))
Full switching at |Vid| = sqrt(2) * Vov(balanced)
Small signal: Iout = Gm*Vid with Gm = gm = sqrt( mu_n*Cox*(W/L)*ISS )

blocks.text: Near Vid = 0 the difference current is a straight line with slope gm; it bends over and clips at ISS where one transistor takes everything. A larger W/L reduces the input range needed to switch fully, so the linear range shrinks as you widen the devices.

With resistor loads RD and a differential output, the gain is Av = -gm*RD (with ro, -gm*(RD||ro)). Because the node at the common source is a virtual AC ground for a symmetric differential input, you can analyse one half of the circuit as a CS stage: this 'half-circuit' trick is the workhorse of differential analysis.
A resistor RS in each source (or a single 2RS) cuts the effective transconductance to gm/(1 + gm*RS), widens the linear input range and lowers gain, just like single-ended degeneration.

blocks.title: Gain and switching range
blocks.text: ISS = 1 mA, mu_n*Cox*W/L = 4 mA/V^2, RD = 5 kohm per side. Find gm, the differential gain, and the Vid that steers all the current.
solution: Balanced: ID = 0.5 mA, Vov = sqrt(2*ID/k) = sqrt(1/4) = 0.5 V, so gm = 2*ID/Vov = 2 mS (check: sqrt(k*ISS) = sqrt(4)=2 mS).
Full switching: Vid = sqrt(2*ISS/k) = sqrt(0.5) = 0.707 V = sqrt(2)*Vov.
blocks.answer: gm = 2 mS, Av = -10, full switching at |Vid| = 0.707 V.
blocks.hint: With equal inputs each side carries ISS/2.

blocks.title: Why is the half-circuit valid?
blocks.text: State the symmetry argument that lets you treat the common-source node as AC ground.
solution: For a purely differential input +v/2 and -v/2 and perfectly matched devices, the current increase in one transistor equals the decrease in the other, so the total current ISS (and hence the voltage at the common source) is unchanged. A node that does not move for a differential signal is a virtual ground.
blocks.answer: Equal and opposite currents cancel, so the tail node does not move.
